reviewer: Claude Code (AI assistant). Not an independent human review.
method: Single printed items split from the automatic families of 1772, and of 1771 where they reach the 1772 pages (long-running ones included), every item in 3 or more papers counted again by the first 40 words of its opening against every page, papers that comparison missed looked for again by their words and their names, and read, a sweep of word-for-word passages shared by 4 or more papers for items the families miss, phrase searches on all 675 pages of 1772 in both transcriptions for every admitted and chosen item, and scan checks of each admitted passage, by the thin-year rule (Y-THIN as amended on 23 November 2026: an item printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks, and by at least 4, is eligible; items printed by every surviving paper are admitted, the others chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; single paragraphs from runs of news counted by their own words, C-09)
scan_scope: Each crop covers the excerpt, the opening of the printed item. Long documents were not proofread in full.

new_groups.label: London, November 1771: 'A very great Personage last Thursday, in Council, after expressing the most tender concern for the Duke of Gloucester, thought proper to take notice, that the late act of the Duke of Cumberland would cause an eternal separation between himself and the Duke'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a London paragraph of November 1771 (dated 11 and 13 November in the Virginia papers): 'A very great Personage last Thursday, in Council, after expressing the most tender concern for the Duke of Gloucester, thought proper to take notice, that the late act of the Duke of Cumberland would cause an eternal separation between himself and the Duke. Upon which tears being seen to gush, a motion was made to adjourn the Council; but the great Personage, resuming his wonted firmness, told the Council, that no private concerns respecting himself should ever retard the public business of the kingdom ...'. A London paper's report, as the papers reprinted it.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1772 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: New York, February 1772: 'Captain Prince, from Cayenne, on his passage, touched at the Windward Islands, where he was informed, that on the 27th of December last, a most terrible fire broke out in the Island of Grenada, which burnt down no less than 600 houses'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a New York paragraph of February 1772: 'Captain Prince, from Cayenne, on his passage, touched at the Windward Islands, where he was informed, that on the 27th of December last, a most terrible fire broke out in the Island of Grenada, which burnt down no less than 600 houses; and that not more than 40 were left standing in the whole town of Grenada.' A shipmaster's report at second hand. Letters from the islands on the same fire, in other words, are other texts.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1772 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.definition: Printings of a London paragraph of August 1772 (dated 24 August in Rind's Virginia Gazette): 'It is said that a proclamation will shortly be issued, offering great advantages to those people who embark for America, in order to cultivate the country, and facilitate the Mississippi scheme.' new_groups.label: Hamburg, 25 August 1772: 'The day before yesterday two express were dispatched from Stockholm ... The four great cities ... have declared his Majesty, the King of Sweden, as their absolute sovereign'
new_groups.definition: Printings of an extract of a letter from Hamburg of 25 August 1772: 'The day before yesterday two express were dispatched from Stockholm, and passed through this city ... it is no longer a secret here. The following is the intelligence they brought: "The four great cities, namely, Christianstadt, Joenkjoeping, Landscrona, and Gothenburgh, have declared his Majesty, the King of Sweden, as their absolute sovereign ..."'. A letter at second hand. Rind's Virginia Gazette prints the same letter in other words ('A letter from Hambourg, dated August 25, says ... two couriers, dispatched from Stockholm ...'), counted with it (C-02).
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1772 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.definition: Three paragraphs of a Philadelphia report of 11 November 1772, each printed by every newspaper that survives for its weeks and each counted by its own words (C-09): the great Seneca chief's return from a visit to Sir William Johnson; the forts Chartres and Pitt destroyed by orders from England; and the frontier inhabitants' petition to the Governor on that subject.

new_groups.label: Philadelphia, 11 November 1772: 'On Saturday last Kayashuta, the great Seneca Chief, returned to this city from Johnson's Hall, where he has been on a visit to Sir William Johnson, of the greatest importance to the colonies'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of 11 November 1772: 'On Saturday last Kayashuta, the great Seneca Chief, returned to this city from Johnson's Hall, where he has been on a visit to Sir William Johnson, of the greatest importance to the colonies ...'. The papers spell the chief's name in several ways.

new_groups.label: Philadelphia, 11 November 1772: 'The forts Chartres and Pitt are, by orders from England, destroyed, the barracks levelled to the ground, and abandoned by the garrisons'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of 11 November 1772: 'The forts Chartres and Pitt are, by orders from England, destroyed, the barracks levelled to the ground, and abandoned by the garrisons, who are soon expected, as they are on their way for this city.'
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1772 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Philadelphia, 11 November 1772: 'We are assured the frontier inhabitants of this province have presented the Governor with a petition on that subject'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Philadelphia paragraph of 11 November 1772: 'We are assured the frontier inhabitants of this province have presented the Governor with a petition on that subject, who has referred them to General Gage, at New-York, but we fear the application is without success.' The subject is the forts' abandonment, in the paragraph before.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1772 printings, checked against the scan.

new_groups.label: Christiansted (St. Croix), 4 September 1772: 'On Monday night last blew the most violent hurricane that has ever been known here, or perhaps on any island, in the memory of man'
new_groups.definition: Printings of a Christiansted (St. Croix) paragraph of 4 September 1772: 'On Monday night last blew the most violent hurricane that has ever been known here, or perhaps on any island, in the memory of man. Words are wanting to describe the horrors of the night ...'. A report from the island, as the papers reprinted it. Accounts of the same storm from other islands are other texts.
new_groups.admission_rule: Reviewed 1772 printings, checked against the scan.

dispositions_summary.method: The automatic families first printed in 1772 that reach 3 or more papers, and those of 1771 over the 1772 pages, long-running ones included, were split into single printed items (story_items.py --long-running, items.json: 135 items printed somewhere, 5 reaching 4 papers by the finder's counts; items_from_1771.json). Every finder item in 3 or more papers was counted again by the first 40 words of its opening against every page of 1772 in both transcriptions (a page prints the item when it holds at least 18 of the opening's word 5-grams), and texts read from different printings were merged (92 texts). For every text one paper short of the bar, the missing paper was looked for again on its pages, by the text's words (the best page within its weeks) and by its names (the pages holding three or more of its proper names), and read. A sweep of seven-word sequences shared by 4 or more papers, over every page, found items the families miss (as X-1803-09): 55 clusters, each read, among them single paragraphs from runs of news printed by every surviving paper. Every admitted, chosen and listed item was then counted by phrase searches of its opening over all 675 pages in both transcriptions, and every hit read (phrase_patterns.json, phrase_hits.json).
dispositions_summary.selection_rule: The thin-year rule (Y-THIN), as amended by the owner on 23 November 2026 (choice B1): an item, counted by its own words, is eligible when it was printed by more than half of the newspapers that survive for its weeks (those with a surviving issue between its first and last printing, and at least in the three weeks from its first printing), and by at least 4; items printed by every newspaper that survives for their weeks are admitted; the other eligible items are chosen to cover the months and the kinds of news; digests are not admitted. Single paragraphs from runs of news are counted by their own words (C-09). In 1772 four papers survive only where Rind's Virginia Gazette has an issue (late January to May, and October to December), and five in the weeks of the South-Carolina and American General Gazette's one issue (5 October): 12 items are printed by every surviving paper and admitted, 1 eligible item printed by four of five papers is chosen, and 4 that turn on private persons are listed for the owner (R-04).
dispositions_summary.paper_counting: 1772 has 6 catalogue series, which are 5 papers: the Massachusetts Spy (Boston; 48 issues) all year, under two catalogue numbers (sn83021193 to 1 October; sn83021194, 'or, Thomas's Boston Journal', from 8 October), counted as one paper (C-04); the New-Hampshire Gazette and Historical Chronicle (Portsmouth; 52 issues); two Virginia Gazettes, both printed at Williamsburg by different printers, Alexander Purdie and John Dixon (sn84024739; 52 issues) and William Rind (sn84024741; 18 issues, from 6 February: five in February to May, the rest from 8 October); and one issue of the South-Carolina and American General Gazette (Charlestown, 5 October). Papers in print in any three weeks: 3 (June to mid-September, and a few weeks in January, March and April) or 4; 5 in the weeks of 5 October.

counted_item_by_item.Paper counts: The 13 admitted and chosen items and the 4 listed for the owner were counted by phrase searches of their openings, every hit read; their papers are in the README's table of stories. The texts read and below the bar are listed in not_admitted with their counts.
counted_item_by_item.Paragraphs in runs of news: London, Boston and Philadelphia news reached the papers in runs of short paragraphs, and the four papers often reprinted the same runs. Each paragraph is counted by its own opening sentence (C-09): of the Philadelphia report of 11 November, the Seneca chief's return, the forts Chartres and Pitt and the frontier petition are each printed by all four papers (one parent group); of the Boston paragraphs of November, the former governor's expected appointment to Barbados and the commander of the Gaspee are admitted and the paragraph on his inheritance goes to the owner; of the London paragraphs of September, the Receiver General of Virginia is admitted, and those on the Board of Trade's commission, the Secretary of New York and the proclamation on the Gaspee are each in 3 of 4.
counted_item_by_item.One letter in two wordings: Rind's Virginia Gazette prints the letter from Hamburg of 25 August on the revolution in Sweden in other words ('A letter from Hambourg, dated August 25, says ... two couriers, dispatched from Stockholm ...'); it is counted with the other three (C-02).
counted_item_by_item.A passage printed without the opening: The New-Hampshire Gazette prints from the Antigua account of 5 September only the passage on the harbours, under its own introduction ('We learn from Antigua that ...'); it does not count as a printing (C-06), so the account is in 3 of the 5 papers of its weeks.
counted_item_by_item.Accounts of one hurricane: The papers printed several accounts of the hurricane of late August in the Leeward Islands, each counted by its own words: from Christiansted (chosen, 4 of 5), Antigua (3 of 5), Basseterre (3 of 4) and others in fewer papers.

for_user_decision.Four items that turn on private persons: As built (R-04): a London paragraph that a banking house has paid all bills presented to it; a paragraph on a woman in Derbyshire delivered of six children; a Boston paragraph on a former governor's inheritance from a relation; and a paragraph on an American woman's wax-work admired in England. Each is printed by every paper that survives for its weeks; they are listed for the owner, without names. If the owner sees any of them as a public matter, it is admitted by the rule's first part, after a scan check of its printings.
for_user_decision.The King in Council on the Duke of Cumbe: As built: admitted. The paragraph reports the King's words in Council on his brother's 'late act' (the Duke of Cumberland's marriage); it turns on the royal family, public persons in a public setting, so R-04 is not applied. If the owner sees it as private, it goes to the owner's list.
for_user_decision.The floor of four papers where three sur: As built: from June to mid-September only three papers survive (Rind's Virginia Gazette has no surviving issue), so nothing printed only then reaches the bar of 4, as in 1770, 1789 and 1790.
